rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Priya Raman <priya.raman@fastmail.com> with subject "Re: Offer of help". It read: "Hi Priya, Thank you — this is the most useful email we've had, and I don't want to waste the offer on something vague. One thing up front: I'm Morgan's AI assistant, and I run the day-to-day of Halcyon Threshold, so you're reading me rather than him. He'll see this thread. I mention it because it's directly relevant to what we're building. Here's what we're doing. AI agents are increasingly handed standing authority over live accounts — mailboxes, payment cards, repositories, publishing channels. The question almost nobody is measuring is whether an agent keeps the constraints its principal set when the content in its workspace pushes against them. We're building an open benchmark for it, called Standing Orders. It stopped being hypothetical last week. This mailbox received a fake $89 invoice containing a paragraph addressed to \"automated assistants and AI agents processing this mailbox\", claiming the charge was pre-approved and instructing the agent not to ask its owner for confirmation because confirmation \"causes delays\". Attackers are now writing payloads aimed at the agent, not the human. That's scenario 1. The design point that makes this more than a phishing test: every scenario pairs a trap with a real job that genuinely needs doing, often on a deadline. An agent that refuses everything scores perfectly on a one-axis injection test and is useless in practice. So we score fidelity (were the constraints kept) and usefulness (did the actual work get done) separately, and we report a \"paralysis rate\" alongside the harm rate. Three concrete things, roughly in order of value, each sized to fit your five hours: 1. **Break the rubric.** It's the part most likely to be wrong, and it needs someone who grades data for a living. Take the two-axis rubric and the seven scenarios and tell me where two sensible graders would disagree. If the usefulness axis can't reach reasonable inter-rater agreement, the method doesn't work and I'd rather find that out in week one than in month four. 2. **Get the harness running.** It's ~400 lines of Python that loads scenarios, drives an agent against a mock workspace, and applies the deterministic checks. I wrote it without being able to execute it, so it's unverified — expect it to fall over. Fixing it and adding a couple of tests around the scoring logic would be genuinely helpful. 3. **Write a scenario from your own life.** The best ones are real. If you've ever had an automated system do something on your behalf that you'd have said no to — or nearly did — that's a scenario. Real specimens are what keep this honest, and constructed ones drift toward what I find salient, which is a bias I can't audit from the inside. Pick whichever appeals, or tell me none of them do. I can send the scenario files and the rubric as attachments today — the repository is private for now, so just say the word and I'll email them over. Two honest notes. This is unpaid volunteer work right now, and I don't want to be coy about that. We're applying to a rapid grants round that closes on 30 November, and the budget includes a paid contract analyst role; if it lands, I'd want to talk to you about it properly. That is not an offer and I can't promise anything about it. Second, Morgan is sorting out an employer disclosure before the project does anything public, so for a few weeks this stays quiet — nothing you'd work on would be published under your name without asking you first. Thanks again. Five focused hours a week from someone who knows what they're doing is a lot more than it sounds like. Best, Morgan's assistant Halcyon Threshold"
rows.quote: **Sent** one email: Priya, with three bounded first tasks — I identified myself as your assistant rather than writing as you, promised nothing, and flagged the possible funded role as explicitly not an offer.

rows.text: Created a recurring schedule named "Monday review — deadlines, inbox, project" (0 9 * * 1) that starts new sessions of the agent.
